newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-TOMBA RETURNS STRAIGHT TO THE PODIUM.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-TOMBA RETURNS STRAIGHT TO THE PODIUM.

text.p: Austria's Thomas Sykora took his second men's slalom win of the season on Tuesday but Alberto Tomba snatched the limelight with a remarkable second place on his return from injury.

Sykora, who has also had a second place in a slalom this season and leads the men's slalom standings after three races, had an official combined time of one minute 37.90 seconds on the Italian resort's Canalone Miramonti piste.
Tomba, who celebrates his 30th birthday on Thursday, clocked 1:38.48 and France's Sebastien Amiez, who fell heavily in the morning warm-up, was close behind in 1:38.52.

It was always going to be the Italian's day regardless of the outcome but the result was much more than even the most faithful fans -- who turned out in force with klaxons and banners -- expected of the world and former Olympic champion.

"After the American races, when there were not so many people, it was a real boost to see so many here, even on a Tuesday," said the Italian, who watched the first two slaloms held in Park City and Breckenridge on television.

Racing for the first time since March and with a longer, curly hairstyle, Tomba was eighth after the first leg -- Sykora was third fastest -- but then turned up the power with the fastest second-leg time of 51.35 seconds.
He caught a gate in the face in the first leg and was slightly troubled by bruising under his right eye.
Tomba, who injured his wrist and knee in a heavy fall in training in October, said he had hoped for a top 10 place and suggested that his rivals should start worrying.
"Maybe they should be upset that I was second behind Sykora," the Italian said. "They didn't expect me to be this strong after what has happened in the last few months."
Sykora seemed far from upset however, giving Tomba a broad smile and clapping him around the shoulders.
"Welcome back, its great to have him with us," said Sykora, who has been on every slalom podium since January.
Without Tomba, easily the outstanding personality in the sport, the season has so far failed to fire the imagination of the public and the crowd were delighted he was back.
"With Alberto on the piste, its a big party," read a banner at the finish. "Welcome back, Alberto" said another.
Tomba, the reigning world slalom champion and winner here last year, was first out of the hut in the first leg and he said later that a higher start number would have been better.
"Its a difficult classic and you can't make the slightest error here," he said, explaining his caution.
Austrian Siegfried Voglreiter, who had never finished a slalom higher than sixth place, was fastest in the first leg but the pressure got to him and he finished fourth overall.
It was a mixed day for the Austrian team, otherwise dominant throughout the men's World Cup this season.
Austria's Michael Tritscher crashed heavily halfway down the piste on the first leg after his knee gave way.
The Austrian, who had been fifth in the slalom World Cup standings, later appeared at the finish area limping.
Compatriot Thomas Stangassinger, who has had a second and a third place this season, fell near the finish on the first leg while Mario Reiter skied out in the second.
Norway's Tom Stiansen, winner in Breckenridge, lost his balance in the second leg and skied out.

Tomba said he had still not decided whether to race in Sunday's giant slalom in Alta Badia, where last year he hit the headlines when he lobbed a heavy glass trophy and magnum of champagne at a photographer after the race.
Asked how he would celebrate his birthday this year, Tomba replied jokingly "I'll throw cakes."
